passage: On the long drive to Grandma's in Porto Alegre, Gabriel turned the radio down and glanced at his son. "Paulo, I want to tell you something before it happens, so it isn't a surprise." Paulo, ten, looked up from his comic. "In the next few years your voice will crack and then get deeper. You'll grow hair under your arms and in other places. You'll sweat more. Girls in your class will start having periods, bleeding once a month, and that's completely normal too." Paulo giggled. "Tiago says..." "Tiago's big brother tells a lot of stories," Gabriel said, smiling. "You can ask me anything, any time, even the awkward stuff." Paulo was quiet for a while, then asked three questions. Gabriel answered each one plainly.

qa.q: What was Paulo reading when Gabriel turned the radio down?
qa.a: His comic.

qa.q: What do Paulo's giggle and then his three questions suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at first, then curious and safe enough to ask.

qa.q: Why is it wise that Gabriel talks before the changes happen?
qa.a: Plain, unhurried words ahead of time give Paulo confidence and replace stories like those from Tiago's brother with facts.

qa.q: What would change if Paulo had only Tiago's big brother's stories to go on?
qa.a: He would learn from rumour and might feel scared or ashamed when his body began changing.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining voice changes, body hair and periods ahead of time in plain, calm words, instead of leaving a child to rumour.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Varun, eleven, nudged his father and snorted at a poster about growing up. "Papa, look, that's gross." Two boys nearby sniggered too. Jatin didn't shush him or laugh. "It's not gross. It's just what bodies do. Want to know what it means?" Varun shrugged, which meant yes. In a low, ordinary voice Jatin explained: voices breaking, hair growing, girls getting periods every month, and that none of it is a joke to the person going through it. "If you hear something at school that sounds strange or scary, bring it to me first." Varun thought. "Mihir said periods mean you're sick." "They don't. They mean a body is growing up normally." When the nurse called his name, Varun was still asking questions.

qa.q: What did Varun snort at?
qa.a: A poster about growing up.

qa.q: What did Varun's shrug suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt a bit embarrassed but curious, and wanted to know without saying so.

qa.q: What did Jatin do instead of shushing or laughing, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He explained calmly and plainly and invited Varun to bring rumours to him first, so Varun learns facts rather than fear.

qa.q: How might a girl in Varun's class feel if boys believed what Mihir said?
qa.a: She might feel ashamed or treated as sick, when her body is simply growing up.

grounding: Illustrates a parent answering a child's giggling with plain, unhurried facts about body changes, so the child learns from a trusted adult rather than rumour.

passage: I'm Jyoti, Ayesha's older sibling, and last Sunday I watched Ammi do something nobody did for me. Ayesha is ten. After lunch Ammi sat her on the divan with a book and a packet of sanitary pads and talked plainly, the way she talks about recipes: what periods are, why they happen, what to do if one starts at school. When Ayesha giggled, Ammi didn't hush her. She waited, then carried on. When Ayesha asked if it hurts, Ammi said, "Sometimes a little. Tell me, and we'll handle it." I couldn't tell exactly what Ayesha felt. She went a bit red. But afterwards she tucked a pad into the inside pocket of her school bag, carefully, like a secret key. I learned from a rumour in Class 7. She won't have to.

qa.q: Where did Ayesha tuck the pad?
qa.a: Into the inside pocket of her school bag.

qa.q: What might Ayesha's red face and careful tucking of the pad suggest?
qa.a: She may have felt a little shy but also prepared, perhaps even proud, treating the pad like a secret key.

qa.q: What made Ammi's explanation work?
qa.a: She spoke early and plainly, didn't giggle or hush, answered the question about pain honestly, and gave a plan for school.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ammi's talk, compared with Jyoti's own experience?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as a gift, since Jyoti learned from a rumour in Class 7 and Ayesha now won't have to.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining periods early in plain, unhurried words, giving a child confidence instead of leaving her to rumour.

passage:
Sunday: On the terrace, flying kites, Yash told Irfan plainly what would happen soon: his voice would crack and deepen, hair would grow in new places, and he might feel moody for no reason. "It's normal, and you can ask me anything." Irfan giggled and threw a pebble. Yash didn't laugh. He just waited, then answered the next question.
A month later: Irfan's voice squeaked in the middle of the class poem. A few boys laughed. Irfan shrugged. "It's breaking. Happens to everyone." He finished the poem.
A few weeks after that: His friend Kabir whispered, panicking, about hair under his arms. "My Abbu told me about that," said Irfan, and explained it the way Yash had.

qa.q: Where did Yash talk to Irfan?
qa.a: On the terrace, flying kites.

qa.q: How did Irfan seem to feel when his voice squeaked in class?
qa.a: He seemed calm and confident, shrugging off the laughter because he already knew what was happening.

qa.q: What made Yash's talk work?
qa.a: He explained before the changes happened, in plain words, didn't laugh at the giggles, and invited questions.

qa.q: How might Kabir feel when Irfan explains?
qa.a: Kabir is probably relieved, going from panic to knowing it is normal.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining voice changes and body hair before they happen, in plain unhurried words, and the child's resulting confidence.

passage: Kiran, you asked why I'm not shy about these things. When I was eleven, in Jabalpur, nobody told me anything. When my period came, I thought I was dying. My friends whispered rumours: don't touch the pickle, it's a punishment. I cried for two days in the bathroom. So when your Mummy turned ten, I sat her down with a cup of tea, the way I'd talk about vegetables, and told her everything plainly: what would happen, why, and what to keep in her bag. She giggled so much she spilled her tea. I didn't laugh, and I didn't stop. The next year, when it came, she walked in and said, "Ma, it's started, I've got it handled." So your Vinita Nani will answer anything you ask.

qa.q: Where did Vinita grow up?
qa.a: In Jabalpur.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel when her period came with no explanation?
qa.a: She was terrified, thinking she was dying, and cried for two days after hearing frightening rumours.

qa.q: What choice did Vinita make when her daughter turned ten, and how did it turn out?
qa.a: She explained everything plainly over tea without laughing or stopping at the giggles, so her daughter later handled her first period calmly.

qa.q: How did Kiran's Mummy respond when her period started?
qa.a: She seemed calm and confident, simply announcing that it had started and she had it handled.

grounding: Shows a parent choosing to explain periods plainly and early, in contrast to the silence and rumour she grew up with, giving her daughter confidence.

passage: Madhuri was leaving at dawn for a three-day school camp, and the bag was still half packed when she came home giggling. 'Ma, Sneha says girls bleed and it hurts like a knife and you can't swim ever again!' Parveen's first instinct was to laugh it off; there was no time tonight. Then the power went out. In the candlelight, folding clothes, Parveen talked plainly and without hurry: that periods come to most girls some time in these years, that it's a normal part of growing up, how pads work, and that the teachers at camp would help. She tucked two pads and spare underwear into a side pocket. 'Just in case. Nothing to be scared of.' Madhuri nodded, curious now, not frightened.

qa.q: What did Parveen tuck into the side pocket?
qa.a: Two pads and spare underwear.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel after the candlelit talk?
qa.a: She felt curious and calm, no longer frightened by the rumours.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Parveen to talk despite the rush?
qa.a: Plain, unhurried facts before camp replaced Sneha's scary rumours and gave Madhuri confidence and a plan.

qa.q: What would change if Parveen had laughed it off?
qa.a: Madhuri would go to camp with only rumours and fear, and might feel alone if her period started there.

grounding: A parent explains periods plainly before they happen, replacing rumour and fear with confidence.
